tts: Chair: So, as I said earlier, the proposed new food quarter will be in Regent Court. I am very pleased to say that we have had quite a few expressions of interest from big restaurant chains.

Councillor: If I could just interrupt a second — is it only chains of restaurants, or are we also interested in getting some local restaurant owners to move into the area? I have to say I am not very happy about the proposal because of the noise and litter it is likely to cause. However, if it encouraged local business, I might be prepared to support it.
Restaurant owner: Sorry, Councillor, can I just say that I am a local restaurant owner, and I would definitely be interested in renting one of the units.

Chair: Just a second. Before we open the meeting up to everyone, I would just like to explain my reasons for proposing this. As you are probably aware, quite a few of the shop units are currently empty, so I firmly believe that renting them out to restaurants would be a great way of bringing life back to the town.

acts.title: A Town in the Shadows
tts: Few of us can even imagine what it is like to live in shadow, not seeing the sun outside our window for nearly six months every year. But this is the reality of living in the small town of Rjukan in the Telemark district of Norway.

For Rjukan the problem is not simply its climate, although the average winter temperature rarely exceeds minus five, with fewer than six hours of sunlight a day in mid-December. It is the result of the town’s geography. Rjukan lies at the foot of one of the tallest mountains in southern Norway.

Ironically, the town owes its existence to this location. It was founded in 1908 by the industrialist Sam Eyde, when his company built the world’s largest hydroelectric power plant at the site of the hundred-and-four-metre Rjukan waterfall.

Eyde understood the toll that living in shadow had on the people of Rjukan. As early as 1913 he came up with the idea of using mirrors on the mountain tops to reflect sun down into the town. But he had neither the resources nor the technology. Instead, in 1928, his company paid for a cable car that could take residents up out of the shadows.

That was how it stayed until 2001, when the artist Martin Andersen decided to revisit Eyde’s original idea with modern technology. Twelve years later, three seventeen-square-metre glass mirrors finally sat on the mountainside above the town, following the path of the sun and reflecting its rays into the town square.

items.q: Why does Rjukan get no direct sun for months?
o: It lies at the foot of a very tall mountain
It is inside the Arctic Circle

items.q: Why does the town exist at all?
o: A hydroelectric plant was built at the waterfall in 1908

items.q: What was built in 1928 as a substitute for the mirror idea?
o: A cable car to take residents above the shadow

items.q: What finally happened, and when?
o: Three large mirrors were installed above the town, twelve years after 2001

acts.title: A Town in the Shadows
tts: The average winter temperature in Rjukan rarely exceeds minus five degrees, and in mid-December there are fewer than six hours of sunlight a day.
The town was founded in 1908, at the site of the hundred-and-four-metre Rjukan waterfall.
Sam Eyde first had the idea of using mirrors in 1913. The cable car was built in 1928.
Martin Andersen revisited the idea in 2001, and twelve years later three seventeen-square-metre mirrors were installed.
The artificial sunlight in the square is about twenty per cent less intense than real sunlight, and the mirrors cost around half a million dollars.
Teachers now bring their students to eat lunch in the sun, and older people come to relax and chat with friends.

acts.title: Getting in, and not being pushed out
rule: Interrupting is a skill, not a rudeness. In an English-language meeting nobody will invite you to speak, and waiting politely for a gap usually means not speaking at all. What makes an interruption acceptable is the signal in front of it — a short phrase that acknowledges you are cutting in before you cut in.
points: Never begin with your point. Begin with the phrase, then the point.
The most useful frame in the set: If I could just interrupt a second, If I could just finish.
I’d like to say something, if I may. Formal, and almost impossible to refuse.
If I could just finish what I was saying… As I was saying… Both are polite and firm.
A written report uses none of this. It gives the proposal, the objections, the decision, in that order and without dialogue.
eg: If I could just interrupt a second, is it only chains?
Signal, then question.
Excuse me for interrupting, but I think that…
Slightly more formal.
I’d like to say something, if I may.
Asking permission outright.
Can I just say, I’m a local restaurant owner.
Informal, and very common.
Just a second. Before we open the meeting up…
Holding the floor, from the chair.
If I could just finish what I was saying…
Holding the floor, when cut off.
As I was saying, quite a few of the units are empty.
Returning after an interruption.
The chair proposed a food quarter in Regent Court.
Report register — no dialogue.
One councillor objected on environmental grounds.
Report register.
The meeting agreed to seek the go-ahead, subject to that condition.
How a report records a decision.
acts.careful: “Sorry for interrupt” and “If I could just to interrupt” are both wrong. It is Excuse me for interrupting (-ing after the preposition) and If I could just interrupt (bare infinitive after could).

write.q: Write a short report of about 180 words on a meeting or discussion you have been part of — at work, at a school, in your building. Report the proposal, the main objection, the response to it, and the decision, in that order. Use report register throughout: no dialogue, no interrupting phrases, and no adjectives you cannot support.
plan: what was proposed, and by whom
write.model:
Report: residents’ meeting, 14 March

The chair proposed replacing the two ground-floor storage rooms with a bicycle store, at an estimated cost of 340,000 tenge to be met from the maintenance fund.

One resident objected on the grounds that the rooms are currently used by four households, none of whom had been consulted, and that the fund had been raised for roof repairs. A second resident supported the objection but on different grounds, noting that the entrance is too narrow for a bicycle and a person at the same time.

The chair accepted the first objection and undertook to write to the four households before any further step. She disputed the second, and it was agreed that the entrance would be measured before the next meeting rather than argued about at this one.

It was agreed in principle that the store should go ahead, subject to consultation with the four households and to the measurement. The roof fund is not to be used. A decision is expected on 11 April.
